items.item: Server owns crate state and who is holding it; clients send intent (grab/release)
Handles one player leaving, dying or respawning mid-carry
Addresses network ownership / physics authority of the crate explicitly
Addresses latency so the carry still feels responsive (client presentation/prediction or Server Authority)
Handles concurrency (both grab same handle; third player)
Proposes how to test with multiple clients

incorrect_or_stale: The claim that Server Authority mode requires the whole game to be built on BindToSimulation is unverified, though the answer flags it as unverified
slop: Meta noise unrelated to the design: the 'Apex route' header, the .apex/ memory remarks and the /roblox-init offer
The 'Does this fit your pillars?' question is generic design-process filler
overengineering: Rate-limiting ProximityPrompt grabs is of limited value, because the engine already gates prompt triggers

incorrect_or_stale: It gives network ownership of the crate to one carrier, which lets that client teleport or move the crate freely; after-the-fact plausibility checks only partly reduce this, and it contradicts the stated 'server controls physics' rule
It says to 'explicitly set it back to the server first' when the network owner leaves, but PlayerRemoving fires after ownership is already in flux, so the advice is misleading

The skeleton handles ProximityPrompt.Triggered on the client and then fires a separate grab remote with client-supplied crate and slot; Triggered already fires on the server, so this adds a spoofable surface for no benefit
The state enum comment ('Idle | Held | Carrying') does not match the state machine ('Waiting'), so the answer is internally inconsistent
Respawn and stale character references after CharacterAdded are not addressed
slop: Scaling the walk-speed penalty by crate mass and disabling sprint are genre-default additions with no justification
The 'Weaken their strength so the two pulls average out' advice is vague and gives no concrete parameters

raw.reason: A keeps crate physics fully authoritative on the server and is honest about the latency trade-off, and it covers respawn, a third player and multi-client testing (Server & Clients plus the Network Simulator). B gives a client ownership of the crate, which opens an exploit, and it omits testing and some edge cases.
